tips.title: Describe the sound, not the artist
tips.body: A listening exam never asks who recorded something. It asks what you can hear. So learn each decade by its **sound** — what instruments, what texture, what the studio was able to do — and the name of the band becomes a detail you can do without.

tips.title: Technology is the fastest clue to a date
tips.body: A drum machine cannot be earlier than the machines existed; a heavily layered vocal cannot predate multi-track recording. When an extract sounds old or new, the reason is nearly always **what the studio could do**, and saying so is worth more than saying it sounds old.

tips.title: Count the bars before you name the form
tips.body: Verse and chorus alternate; a twelve-bar blues repeats every twelve bars. You can tell which you are hearing within one or two passes of the pattern by counting, and the answer to a structure question follows immediately.

tips.title: The backbeat is on 2 and 4
tips.body: Almost every popular style since the 1950s puts the snare drum on beats **2 and 4** of a four-four bar. Those are the beats classical music treats as weak, which is exactly why the sound is driving rather than stately. Tap it and check before you write anything about rhythm.

tips.title: Twelve-bar blues: 4, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2
tips.body: Count the bars on each chord: four of **I**, two of **IV**, two of **I**, one of **V**, one of **IV**, two of **I**. The numbers add to twelve, and chord I takes 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 of them.

why.matters: The listening exam never asks who recorded a track. It asks what you can hear, and it will hand you a popular extract you have never heard and expect you to describe it at speed. Each decade could do something the last one could not, almost always because the instruments or the studio changed, and that is the fastest way to date an extract from its sound alone: not names and chart positions, but which tool is audible. This topic is that vocabulary, decade by decade, from a band playing live in mono to a voice tuned in software.

examples.title: The record that holds more than the band can play
examples.body: Multitrack recording let parts be added one at a time instead of played together, so a record could contain more music than the band could make in a room. *Killer Queen* is a set work partly for that reason: vocal harmonies overdubbed until a few singers sound like a choir, and a guitarist in three-part harmony with himself. Hear a chorus that no group of people could sing live and you are almost certainly in the 1960s or later; hear a whole song that plainly happened in one room, in mono, and you are earlier.

examples.title: Why the beat stopped breathing
examples.body: A human drummer pushes a little into a chorus and settles again; a drum machine keeps perfect time, forever, and you can hear the difference. So can a snare given a huge artificial reverb, and a part that repeats exactly because it was sequenced rather than played. Those sounds date a track to the 1980s or later as surely as a haircut dates a photograph. The device is the evidence; the year follows from it.

visual.alt: A table contrasting a human drummer, whose timing drifts and whose repeats differ, with a drum machine, exact every bar and identical on every repeat, with a big artificial reverb on the snare

examples.title: Dating a song in ten seconds
examples.body: Ask one question of the extract: what can I hear that could not have existed earlier? A twelve-bar blues band in mono says the 1950s. Stacked vocal harmony says the 1960s onwards. A synthesiser bass and a machine on the drums say the 1980s. A fragment of another record looping underneath says the 1990s. A voice with its pitch nudged into place says this century. You are not guessing the artist; you are reading the equipment.

steps.title: Why a listening exam cares about pop
steps.body:
Popular styles run through Edexcel's areas of study. **Vocal Music** holds Queen's *Killer Queen*, released in **1974**; **Music for Stage and Screen** holds a musical theatre song, *Defying Gravity*; and **Fusions** holds two tracks that fuse popular styles with other traditions. Section A's unfamiliar extract, which is closely related to a set work, can be a popular one, and Section B compares a set work with an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study: in 2019 it set *Release* against Panjabi MC's *Mundian To Bach Ke*.

So this topic is not history for its own sake. It is the vocabulary you need to describe a popular record at speed.

> The exam never asks who recorded something. It asks what you can hear.

That changes what is worth learning. Not names and chart positions, but **what changed in the sound**, decade by decade, and **why** — which is almost always because the instruments or the studio changed.

Pearson's suggested wider listening for Vocal Music includes two popular tracks: the Beach Boys' *God Only Knows*, from *Pet Sounds* (1966), and ABBA's *Super Trouper* (1980). Hearing what separates them is exactly the skill this topic builds.

steps.title: Decade by decade, by what changed in the sound
steps.body:
Every row below is a change in **what you can hear**, and nearly all of them come from a change in equipment.

**The 1950s.** Rock emerged in this decade as **rock and roll**. A small band: voice, electric guitar, double bass or bass guitar, drums, often piano or saxophone. The **twelve-bar blues** underneath a great deal of it. Recording is in **mono** and largely live, so what you hear is what happened in the room.

**The 1960s.** The four-piece band settles: drums, bass, two guitars, everybody singing. **Multi-track recording** becomes normal, which changes everything — parts can be added one at a time instead of played together, so a record can contain more than a band can play. **Vocal harmony** thickens.

**The 1970s.** The studio becomes an instrument in its own right. *Killer Queen*, from **1974**, is a set work precisely because of what it does with **multi-tracking**: layered vocal harmonies that no group of people could sing live. Elsewhere, longer tracks, guitar solos, string sections, and in disco a steady bass drum on every beat — **four on the floor**.

**The 1980s.** **Synthesisers** and **drum machines**. A drum machine keeps perfect time, which is audible: the beat stops breathing. Big artificial reverb on the snare. Sequencing means a part can repeat exactly, forever.

**The 1990s.** **Sampling**: a fragment of an existing recording becomes an instrument. Dance music built on a **loop** rather than on a chord sequence. Vocal writing becomes more **melismatic** in R&B.

**The 2000s onwards.** Everything happens inside software. **Pitch shift** correction on voices, **chorus** and other effects applied after the fact, and the basic unit of composition becomes the loop rather than the verse.

One thread runs through all of it: **each decade can do something the last one could not**, and that is usually the fastest way to date an extract.

The group must have had a very large number of singers
The harmonies were added by a synthesiser rather than sung
It tells you nothing useful about when it was recorded
check.solution: **Multi-track recording** lets each part be recorded separately and laid over the others, so a record can contain more voices than exist. It is the reason *Killer Queen* sounds the way it does. A few 1950s records experimented with overdubbing, but layered vocals became normal in the 1960s. Technology is the fastest clue to a date, because a record cannot use equipment that was not yet in use.

steps.title: The band, named properly
steps.body:
A popular music line-up has a standard shape, and each part has a job. Name the instrument and the job, and an instrumentation question is finished.

- **Lead vocal** — the tune and the words. A **backing vocal** supports it, often in harmony.
- **Electric guitar** — chords, riffs or a solo. Distorted or clean; techniques include **bends**, **hammer ons**, **pull offs** and **slides**.
- **Bass guitar** — the lowest line, tying the harmony to the rhythm. A **riff** in the bass drives a whole track.
- **Drum kit** — bass drum, snare, hi-hat, toms and cymbals. The **snare on 2 and 4** is the backbeat.
- **Keyboard** — piano, electric piano, organ, or a **synthesiser**, which makes sounds electronically rather than mechanically.
- **Additional forces** — brass or string sections, hand percussion, a choir.

And the studio, which is not a person but belongs in the same list:

- **Multi-track recording** — each part on its own track, recorded separately.
- **Overdubbing** — adding to a finished recording.
- **Double tracking** — the same part recorded twice and laid over itself, which thickens and slightly blurs it.
- **Reverb** — artificial space. **Delay** — audible repeats.
- **Chorus effect** — several copies at slightly different pitch and timing, as though more than one person were playing.
- **Flanger** — two identical signals, one slightly delayed by a changing amount, giving a sweeping sound.
- **Pitch shift** — the recorded pitch raised or lowered.
- **Sampling** — a piece of another recording used as material.

Terms like these belong to the specification's Music Vocabulary List (Appendix 3), which the examiners' report tells students to learn.

check.prompt: The same vocal line has clearly been recorded twice and the two takes laid over each other, thickening the sound. Give the two-word term for this.
check.solution: **Double tracking**. It is a studio effect: the same part performed twice and the recordings played together, which thickens the sound and slightly blurs it because the two takes are never identical. It cannot be reproduced live by one singer, which is often the point.

steps.title: The shape of a song
steps.body:
Two structures cover most popular music, and you can tell them apart by counting.

**Verse and chorus.** The **verse** carries the story and its words change each time. The **chorus** carries the hook and its words come back unchanged. That is the test: if the words return, it is the chorus.

Around them sit optional sections, and each has a name worth knowing:

- **Intro** — before the singing starts.
- **Pre-chorus** — a short link that builds into the chorus.
- **Middle eight** or **bridge** — a contrasting section, usually once, usually after the second chorus.
- **Instrumental** or **solo** — the band without the singer.
- **Outro** — the ending, often a **fade**.

*Killer Queen* is built this way: verses and choruses alternating, with an instrumental after the first chorus, a guitar solo before the third verse, and an outro that fades.

**Twelve-bar blues.** Twelve bars, repeating, using only chords **I**, **IV** and **V**:

| Bars | 1–4 | 5–6 | 7–8 | 9 | 10 | 11–12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chord | I | IV | I | V | IV | I |

In C major that is C, F, G and nothing else. Chord I fills 8 of the twelve bars. Bars 9 to 12 (V, IV, I, I) make the last line, and the final two bars, which lead back to the start, are called the **turnaround**.

**The four-chord song.** An enormous number of popular songs sit on **I, V, vi, IV** — in C major, C, G, A minor, F. Three major chords and one minor, which is why the progression can sound bright and wistful at once.

props.title: The twelve-bar blues, bar by bar

visuals.alt: A table giving the chord in each bar of a twelve-bar blues, as a roman numeral and as a chord in C major

visuals.problem: An extract repeats a chord pattern every twelve bars, going to a second chord at bar 5 and a third at bar 9. What is it, and what are the chords?

steps.text: Twelve bars, repeating, is the twelve-bar blues.
steps.note: Counting is the whole test. Verse and chorus sections are not usually twelve bars long and do not repeat that exactly.

steps.text: The chord at bar 5 is chord IV.
steps.note: In the standard pattern bars 1 to 4 are chord I and bars 5 to 6 are chord IV.

steps.text: The chord at bar 9 is chord V, which begins the last line of the pattern.
steps.note: Bar 10 falls back to IV and bars 11 and 12 return to chord I ready for the next repetition.

steps.text: In C major: C, F and G.
steps.note: All three are major chords, because the blues uses I, IV and V of a major scale.

check.prompt: In a song, one section returns three times with exactly the same words each time. What is it?
check.solution: The **chorus** is the section whose words come back unchanged — that is the test, and it is more reliable than volume or energy. A verse keeps its music but changes its words; a middle eight usually appears once; an intro comes before the singing starts.

markScheme.description: the chorus

steps.title: Rhythm: the backbeat and what sits against it
steps.body:
Most popular music since the 1950s has four beats in a bar, usually **four-four**: four crotchet beats. (*Killer Queen* is mainly in 12/8, four dotted-crotchet beats, and the backbeat still falls on 2 and 4.) What makes it sound like popular music rather than like a march is where the stress goes.

**The backbeat.** The snare drum lands on beats **2 and 4**. In classical music those are the weak beats of the bar, so putting the loudest sound of the kit on them inverts the usual stress. Tap four beats and clap on the second and fourth: that is the sound of every style in this topic.

**Four on the floor.** The bass drum on **every** beat, 1, 2, 3 and 4. Disco made it famous and it is still the signature of dance music. It does not replace the backbeat; the snare is still on 2 and 4 on top of it.

**Syncopation.** A stressed note landing where the bar would normally be weak — often on the *off*beat, the half-beat between the numbers. Bass lines and vocal lines are syncopated far more often than drum parts.

**Swung rhythm.** Two notes written equal but played long-then-short. *Killer Queen* has a swung feel throughout. Swing came into popular music from jazz.

**Anacrusis.** A phrase that begins before the bar line, on an upbeat. Every verse and chorus of *Killer Queen* starts with one, and hearing it is a real observation about a real set work.

These four are not alternatives. A single track can be in four-four with a backbeat, four on the floor underneath, a syncopated bass and a swung vocal, all at once.

steps.title: Melody, harmony and the words
steps.body:
**The hook** is the bit you cannot get rid of. It is usually short, usually in the chorus, and usually repeated. Naming it is worth a mark; saying *why* it sticks — a leap, a repeated note, a syncopation, an unexpected chord underneath — is worth more.

**Syllabic and melismatic.** One note to a syllable is **syllabic**; many notes to one syllable is a **melisma**. Popular singing is often syllabic in the verse, with melismas saved for the chorus, and the contrast between the two is a real observation.

**Riff and ostinato.** A short pattern repeated at the same pitch is an **ostinato**; in popular styles the same thing is called a **riff**. If it repeats at a *different* pitch it is a **sequence** instead, which is a different word and a different mark.

**Harmony.** Popular songs mostly use ordinary major and minor triads, with three habits worth knowing:

- **Added sevenths** and other extended chords, which come from jazz and give a richer, less settled sound.
- **A repeated chord sequence** under a whole section, so the interest lives in the voice.
- **Blue notes**: flattened thirds and sevenths borrowed from the blues, sung against a major chord.

**Words.** Use the right word: in popular styles they are usually called **lyrics**; in Western classical vocal music, the *text* or the *words*. And when the music illustrates what a word means — rising notes on *rising* — that is **word painting**, in a pop song exactly as in Purcell.

**The fade.** An ending that gets quieter rather than stopping. It is a recording-studio ending, impossible live, and worth naming when you hear it.

check.prompt: A singer stretches one syllable of a word over eleven separate notes. Give the term for this.
check.solution: A **melisma**: a group of notes used to set just one syllable of text. The opposite is **syllabic** writing, one note per syllable. Popular verses are often syllabic, with melismas saved for the chorus, and the contrast between them is worth pointing out.

steps.title: Your turn: date an extract from its sound
steps.body:
Here are three descriptions. For each, decide roughly when it was made and say **which feature told you**. The feature matters more than the date.

**A.** A four-piece band. Drums with the snare on 2 and 4, bass guitar, two electric guitars, one singing lead and the others adding harmony behind. Twelve bars of chords I, IV and V repeating. The whole thing sounds as though it happened in one room at one time.

**B.** A steady bass drum on all four beats. A synthesiser holds long chords; another plays a repeating pattern that never varies by a hair. The snare has a huge artificial space around it that stops abruptly. No guitar anywhere.

**C.** A two-bar drum pattern that is clearly a fragment of an older recording, repeating under everything. A voice, heavily melismatic in the chorus and syllabic in the verse. Strings that were never played by a string section.

Write one sentence for each: the decade, and the feature that decided it. Then check yourself against the answers.

check.prompt: Extract B has a repeating synthesiser pattern that never varies by a hair, and a snare with a huge artificial space that stops abruptly. Which decade does that point to?
check.solution: A pattern with no variation at all means a **sequencer or drum machine**, and a large artificial reverb that cuts off abruptly is a studio treatment strongly associated with the **1980s**. Neither is possible in the 1940s or 1950s, and neither is characteristic of the 1960s. The reasoning is always the same: what could the equipment of the time actually do?

steps.title: Going deeper: writing about a popular extract
steps.body:
The difference between a weak answer and a strong one about popular music is rarely knowledge. It is precision, and joining the feature to its effect.

| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| It has a good beat | The snare on beats 2 and 4 gives it a steady drive |
| Lots of instruments | Drum kit, bass guitar, two electric guitars and layered backing vocals |
| It sounds like the eighties | A drum machine and synthesiser pads, so the beat is perfectly even |
| The singer is really good | The verse is syllabic and the chorus melismatic, so the chorus sounds like a release |
| The chorus is catchy | The hook repeats a three-note figure over an unchanging four-chord loop |
| It has effects on it | The lead vocal is double tracked, and there is audible delay on the guitar |

Three habits are worth building now, because they carry into every set work.

**Say what the studio did, as well as what the players did.** In popular music since the 1960s, some of what you hear was never performed. Double tracking, sampling, a drum machine and a fade are all things the *recording* does, and they are part of the vocabulary you are expected to identify.

**Watch for a fusion.** If an extract sounds like two traditions at once — a Punjabi drum under a dance beat, a jazz harmony under a Brazilian rhythm — say so, name both traditions, and name a feature from each. That is exactly what the Fusions set works are marked on.

**Do not date a recording by how old it sounds.** Date it by what it does that an earlier decade could not.

options: There are lots of studio effects used on the vocals in this recording
The singing has clearly been treated in some way in the studio
The lead vocal is double tracked, which thickens it and makes the chorus sound bigger
The vocals sound really full and powerful in the chorus section
check.solution: It names the effect — double tracking — and then says what it does. The other three describe an impression without naming any feature, so there is nothing for the knowledge half of a mark scheme to credit, and nothing for the appraisal half to rest on.

steps.title: What to carry forward
steps.body:
- The exam asks what you can **hear**, never who recorded it.
- Each decade could do something the last could not, and **technology dates a recording** faster than anything else: mono, multi-tracking, drum machines, sampling, software.
- Name the **line-up** exactly: drum kit, bass guitar, electric guitar, lead and backing vocals, keyboard or synthesiser.
- The **studio counts**: multi-track recording, overdubbing, double tracking, reverb, delay, chorus, flanger, pitch shift, sampling, the fade.
- **Verse and chorus** is the commonest form. The chorus is the section whose words come back unchanged.
- The **twelve-bar blues** is 12 bars of chords I, IV and V — in C major, C, F and G.
- Many songs sit on **I, V, vi, IV**: in C major, C, G, A minor, F.
- Rhythm: **backbeat** on 2 and 4, **four on the floor** on all four, **syncopation** off the beat, **swung** rhythm long-then-short.
- Voices: **syllabic** against **melismatic**, the **hook**, **lyrics** rather than words, **blue notes**.
- *Killer Queen*, 1974, is the set work all of this leads to.

check.prompt: How many bars are there in one cycle of a twelve-bar blues, and which chords does it use?
options: Twelve bars, using chords I, V, vi and IV
Eight bars, using chords I, IV and V
Sixteen bars, using every chord of the key
Twelve bars, using chords I, IV and V
check.solution: The name says the length: **12 bars**. The pattern uses only chords **I, IV and V**, with chord I filling 8 of them and chord V arriving at bar 9. I, V, vi, IV is the four-chord pop progression, which is a different thing.

markScheme.description: twelve bars of I, IV and V

questions.prompt: In a four-four bar of popular music, where does the snare drum of the backbeat land?
questions.solution: The **backbeat** puts the snare on beats **2 and 4** — the beats classical music treats as weak. Beats 1 and 3 usually carry the bass drum; the bass drum on all four is **four on the floor**; notes between the beats are off-beats and make for syncopation.

markScheme.description: beats 2 and 4

questions.prompt: Which section of a song has the same words every time it returns?
questions.solution: The **chorus** returns with its words unchanged, which is the reliable test. A verse keeps its music and changes its words; a middle eight is a contrasting section usually heard once; an instrumental has no words at all.

markScheme.description: the chorus

questions.prompt: Give the term for a short musical pattern repeated over and over at the same pitch in a popular song.
questions.solution: A **riff**, which is the popular-music word for an **ostinato**: a short pattern repeated throughout a section. If the pattern came back at a *different* pitch it would be a **sequence** instead.

markScheme.description: riff

questions.prompt: A recording contains far more vocal harmony parts than there were singers in the group. What made that possible?
options: A very large choir was brought in for the session
The singers each sang two notes at the same time
A synthesiser played the extra harmony parts instead
Multi-track recording, with each part recorded separately
questions.solution: **Multi-track recording** puts each part on its own track, recorded one at a time, so a record can hold more parts than there are people. It is why *Killer Queen* sounds as it does, and it is the reason records from the 1960s onwards can do things no band could do live.

markScheme.description: multi-track recording

questions.prompt: A twelve-bar blues in C major uses three chords. Which three?
options: C, E minor and A minor
questions.solution: The blues uses chords **I, IV and V** only. In C major those are **C, F and G**, and all three are major. C, G and A minor belong to the four-chord pop progression I, V, vi, IV; the other two lists include chords the blues does not use.

markScheme.description: C, F and G

questions.prompt: The bass drum lands on all four beats of every bar. What is that called?
questions.solution: **Four on the floor**: the bass drum on every beat. Disco made it famous, and it is still the signature of dance music. It sits *underneath* the backbeat rather than replacing it, so the snare is usually still on 2 and 4 on top of it.

markScheme.description: four on the floor

questions.prompt: A fragment of an existing recording is taken and used as material in a new track. Give the one-word term.
questions.solution: **Sampling**. It became widespread in the late 1980s and 1990s and changed how records were made: a drum pattern or a string chord from an older recording becomes an instrument in a new one, so a track can contain playing that nobody in the room did.

markScheme.description: sampling

questions.prompt: Two synthesiser parts repeat for four minutes without varying by the smallest amount. What does that tell you about how the track was made?
options: It was sequenced, so a machine is playing rather than a person
The players were unusually accurate on the day of the recording
The same two bars were copied and pasted by hand afterwards
It tells you nothing, since people can play very evenly
questions.solution: A human performance always varies slightly. Playing with **no** variation at all means a **sequencer** or **drum machine** is producing it, which is one of the clearest signals of the 1980s onwards. The point generalises: what you can hear tells you what equipment was in the room.

markScheme.description: a sequencer or drum machine, not a player

questions.prompt: A singer is syllabic through the verse and then stretches single syllables over many notes in the chorus. What is the second of those called?
questions.solution: **Melismatic** writing sets one syllable over a group of notes; **syllabic** writing gives one note to each syllable. The contrast between a syllabic verse and a melismatic chorus is a real observation about a real song, and it is worth making.

markScheme.description: melismatic

questions.prompt: Popular songs often sit on the chord pattern I, V, vi, IV. Name the chord that vi would be in C major.
questions.solution: Chord vi of C major is built on the sixth degree, **A**, and comes out minor, so it is **A minor**. The full progression in C is C, G, A minor, F — three major chords and one minor, which is why it can sound bright and wistful at the same time.

markScheme.description: A minor

questions.prompt: Put these changes in popular music into the order they happened.
items: Records are made in mono, largely live in one room
Multi-track recording lets each part be added separately
The studio becomes an instrument, with layered vocal harmonies
Drum machines and synthesisers make the beat perfectly even
Sampling turns fragments of old recordings into new material
questions.solution: Mono and live came first, because nothing else was possible. Multi-tracking arrived next and made everything after it possible: once parts can be recorded separately, a record can hold more than a band can play, which is what the layered records of the 1970s do — *Killer Queen*, from 1974, among them. Drum machines and synthesisers follow in the 1980s, and sampling in the late 1980s and 1990s. The order is not arbitrary: each step needs the one before it.

markScheme.description: mono and live before multi-tracking
multi-tracking before the layered studio records
drum machines before sampling

questions.prompt: A pattern is stated, then immediately repeated a tone higher. Which term applies?
questions.solution: Repetition at a **different pitch** is a **sequence**. A riff and an ostinato both repeat at the *same* pitch, which is the distinction the mark scheme is testing; double tracking is a studio effect and not a melodic device at all.

markScheme.description: sequence

questions.prompt: A band in 1955 records the usual way for the time: everyone plays at once onto a single track, with no overdubbing. Which of these could they NOT do on that recording?
options: Putting the snare drum on beats 2 and 4
Playing a twelve-bar blues on chords I, IV and V
Laying eight separate vocal takes over one another
Ending the song by fading it out in the studio
questions.solution: Stacking eight separate takes needs the parts recorded one after another, which a single-track session played live cannot do; that is why records made that way sound like a band in a room. A backbeat and a twelve-bar blues are things players do, not things equipment does, and a fade can be made on a single-track recording simply by turning the level down.

markScheme.description: the option requiring multi-track recording

questions.prompt: A song is built on a repeating twelve-bar blues in four-four time. The extract plays the pattern through four times without a break. How many crotchet beats is that in total?
questions.solution: One cycle is **12 bars**, and four-four holds **4 crotchets** a bar, so one cycle is 48 beats. Four cycles is 48 times 4, which is **192** crotchet beats.

markScheme.description: 12 bars times 4 beats times 4 cycles = 192

questions.prompt:
An extract of popular music is played several times.

**What you hear:**

- Four crotchets in a bar. The snare drum lands on the second and fourth beats of every bar.
- Drum kit, bass guitar, two electric guitars and a lead singer, with the other players adding harmony behind him.
- The chord pattern repeats every twelve bars: four bars on one chord, two on a second, two on the first again, then one bar on a third chord, one back on the second, and two to finish on the first.
- A saxophone plays a solo over the same twelve bars.
- The recording sounds as though everyone played at once in the same room; nothing is layered.

Describe this extract, referring to its instrumentation, structure, rhythm and how it was recorded, and say roughly when it was made and why.
questions.solution:
**Instrumentation.** A standard small band of the period: **drum kit**, **bass guitar**, **two electric guitars** and a **lead vocal**, with the other players supplying **backing vocal harmony**. A **saxophone** takes a solo. That combination — guitars and a saxophone together — is characteristic of early rock and roll, where the saxophone was still doing the job the lead guitar later took over.

**Structure.** The chord pattern described is the **twelve-bar blues**: four bars of chord **I**, two of **IV**, two of **I**, then one bar of **V**, one of **IV**, and two of **I** to finish. Only chords **I, IV and V** appear, which is what makes it a blues rather than simply a repeating pattern. In C major those chords would be C, F and G. The saxophone solo runs over the same twelve bars rather than over a new section, which is standard: in a blues the solo is another chorus of the same structure.

**Rhythm.** Four crotchets in a bar with the **snare on beats 2 and 4** is the **backbeat**. Those are the beats that would be weak in classical music, so putting the loudest sound of the kit on them inverts the usual stress and is what makes the music drive rather than march. It is the single most consistent feature of popular music from the 1950s onwards.

**Recording and date.** Everything sounds as though it happened at once in one room, and nothing is layered. That means the recording was made **live**, before **multi-track recording** made it normal to add parts separately, so the extract is from the **1950s or very early 1960s**. The reasoning is about equipment rather than about atmosphere: a record cannot use a technique that did not yet exist, so the absence of layering is evidence and the fact that it "sounds old" is not.

**Overall.** Every feature points the same way. The twelve-bar blues, the small band with a saxophone, the backbeat and the unlayered recording all belong to the decade in which rock and roll emerged.

questions.prompt:
An extract of popular music is played several times.

**What you hear:**

- Four crotchets in a bar at a fast tempo, with the bass drum on every one of them.
- A synthesiser holds long sustained chords; a second synthesiser plays a two-bar pattern that repeats without the slightest variation.
- The snare has a large artificial space around it which cuts off abruptly rather than dying away.
- A lead vocal, syllabic in the verse and stretching the title word over nine notes in the chorus. The lead vocal has plainly been recorded twice and the takes laid over one another.
- The chord symbols printed above the vocal line for the chorus are C | G | Am | F, repeating.
- The track does not end; it gets quieter and quieter until it disappears.

Describe this extract, referring to its instrumentation and production, its rhythm, its melody and its harmony.
questions.solution:
**Instrumentation and production.** There are no acoustic instruments at all. **Synthesisers** hold sustained chords and play the repeating pattern, and that pattern is **sequenced** — a two-bar pattern that repeats "without the slightest variation" is not something a player produces. The drums could be a **drum machine** or a real kit: a gated snare was used on both, so it does not settle the question. The snare carries a large artificial **reverb** that stops abruptly rather than dying away, a treatment strongly associated with the 1980s. The lead vocal is **double tracked**: recorded twice and the takes laid over one another, which thickens it and slightly blurs it. The track ends with a **fade**, an ending made at the mixing desk rather than played.

**Rhythm.** The bass drum on all four beats is **four on the floor**, which disco made famous and which remains the signature of dance music. Against it, the perfect regularity of the synthesiser pattern removes every trace of human timing, so the beat does not breathe. That is not a criticism: it is what the style is for, and it is the reason the track can run for minutes without the pulse ever wavering.

**Melody.** The verse is **syllabic**, one note to each syllable, and the chorus stretches the title word over **nine notes**, which is a **melisma**. Setting a narrow, conversational verse against a melismatic chorus makes the chorus sound like a release, and it is one common way popular songs mark the arrival of the hook.

**Harmony.** The loop starts on C and uses only chords of C major, so the key is most likely **C major**, and the printed chorus chords read as **I, V, vi, IV** — C, G, A minor, F. Three major chords and one minor, which is why the progression sounds bright and slightly wistful at once. It **repeats unchanged** for the whole chorus, so the harmony asks for no attention at all and every bit of interest has to come from the voice and the production. That is a deliberate choice rather than a limitation.

**Overall.** Everything here was made in a studio rather than performed in a room: synthesised sound, machine timing, a doubled voice, an engineered ending, over a chord loop that never moves. Taken together the features place the extract in the **1980s**: the sequencing and the gated snare are things an earlier decade could not have done.

questions.prompt: What is the usual term for the words of a popular song?
questions.solution: In popular styles the words are the **lyrics**. In Western classical vocal music the usual terms are the *text* or the *words*, and a libretto is the whole text of an opera or a musical — so using the right one is a small, free mark.

markScheme.description: lyrics

questions.prompt: An extract has a Punjabi drum playing under a four on the floor dance beat, with a sung melody in a folk style. What should an answer call this?
options: A fusion, naming a feature from each tradition
Dance music, because the beat is the loudest element
Folk music, because the melody comes from a folk style
A medley, because two kinds of music are used in it
questions.solution: A **fusion** brings together two or more distinct traditions **so that each stays audible** — which is exactly what is described. Calling it by one of its ingredients throws away half the answer. A medley would put the two styles one after the other; a fusion has them at the same time.

markScheme.description: a fusion, with a feature named from each tradition

questions.prompt:
A student writes this about an extract of popular music:

> "This is a pop song from quite a long time ago. It has a really good beat that makes you want to dance, and lots of instruments playing at the same time. The singer is very good and the chorus is really catchy. There are a lot of effects on it. I think it is from the eighties because it sounds old."

Explain what is wrong with this answer, and rewrite it so that every point names a musical feature and says what it does.
questions.solution:
**What is wrong.**

**Nothing is named.** "Lots of instruments" names none of them; "a lot of effects" names none of those either. A mark scheme credits *drum kit, bass guitar, distorted electric guitar and double-tracked backing vocals*, and it credits *reverb* and *delay*. It cannot credit a plural.

**The judgements have nothing underneath them.** "A really good beat", "the singer is very good", "the chorus is really catchy" are all impressions. An appraising point is only credited where a musical observation supports it, so each of these earns nothing as it stands — not because the impressions are wrong, but because nothing explains them.

**The date is argued backwards.** "It sounds old" is not evidence. A recording is dated by what it *does*: whether it is layered, whether the timing is machine-perfect, whether anything in it has been sampled. And "quite a long time ago" and "the eighties" are two different claims in the same answer.

**No structure at all.** The answer mentions a chorus without saying what makes it one, and never says whether the song is in verse and chorus form, a twelve-bar blues, or anything else.

**Rewritten.**

> The extract is in four-four with the **snare on beats 2 and 4** — a **backbeat** — and the bass drum on all four, which is **four on the floor**, so the pulse is steady and insistent and the track drives rather than marches.
>
> The forces are **drum kit, bass guitar, electric guitar and lead vocal**, with **backing vocals in harmony** behind the chorus. The lead vocal has been **double tracked**, which thickens it, and there is audible **delay** on the guitar, so some of what is heard was made at the desk rather than played.
>
> The song is in **verse and chorus** form: the chorus returns twice with the same words, and its **hook** is a short repeated figure over a **four-chord loop** that never changes, so all the interest sits in the voice. The verse is **syllabic** and the chorus **melismatic**, which is what makes the chorus sound like a release.
>
> The **drum machine** timing is perfectly even and the snare carries a large artificial **reverb** that cuts off abruptly, so the recording is from the **1980s** — not because it sounds old, but because neither was in common use before the 1980s.

**Why the rewrite earns.** Every sentence now names something a mark scheme lists, and every judgement is attached to the feature that causes it. The date is argued from the equipment rather than from the atmosphere, and the structure is named and then justified by the return of the words.

examTechnique.body:
**This topic is preparation, not a set work.** The Edexcel exam does not ask "describe the 1980s". It asks you to appraise an extract, and an extract of popular music is much easier to describe when you already know what popular music does.

**Name the element, then the effect.** *Electric guitar with distortion, so the sound is aggressive* earns more than either half alone.

**Structure first.** Verse and chorus is the commonest popular form, and naming it costs one word. Listen for the return: the chorus is the part that comes back with the same words.

**The studio counts as an instrument.** Double tracking, reverb, delay, multi-track recording, sampling, a drum machine — these are the terms to name, and the examiners' report points students to the specification's vocabulary list for them.

**Be specific about the band.** *Drum kit, bass guitar, electric guitar and lead vocal* is an answer about instrumentation. *Instruments* is not.

**Watch the rhythm.** Syncopation, swung rhythm and the backbeat are three different things and they often appear together.

**Popular vocal writing has its own vocabulary.** Syllabic and melismatic, the **hook**, the **riff**, **lyrics** rather than *words*, and **ad libs** over a fade.

**When a piece sounds like two styles at once, say so.** That is a fusion, and it earns credit in Section B where it is relevant.
examinerErrors: Naming the band or the song rather than describing what can be heard.
Calling every repeated idea a riff, when a riff is specifically a melodic or rhythmic pattern repeated at the same pitch.
Saying "drums and guitar" where a mark scheme wants the instruments named precisely: "drum kit, bass guitar and distorted electric guitar".
Describing an effect — "it sounds happy" — without naming the feature that causes it.
Confusing verse and chorus, when the chorus is the section whose words come back unchanged.
Ignoring the production entirely, although studio effects are part of the vocabulary you are expected to use.
Assuming a piece is old because the recording is quiet, rather than because of what is playing.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer describes what it can hear rather than what it can name. It gives the line-up precisely — drum kit, bass guitar, electric guitar, lead and backing vocals — and says what the studio is doing as well as what the players are. It hears the structure as it goes, counting the return of the chorus, and it knows that a twelve-bar blues is twelve bars of chords I, IV and V rather than a general feeling of bluesiness. It places a date on a recording from what the technology of the time could do, and says so.
